THOUGHT: The patient has the classic triad of an ovarian mass, ascites, and a right-sided pleural effusion causing dyspnea. Differential includes ovarian carcinoma with malignant ascites/pleural spread, benign ovarian stromal tumors (classically fibroma/fibrothecoma) causing Meigs syndrome, and less likely systemic causes of effusion/ascites (cardiac, hepatic, renal) which are not supported by the history or exam. Supporting features for a benign Meigs-type process: relatively young but otherwise well-appearing patient without constitutional symptoms, normal CBC, a large unilateral ovarian mass on ultrasound, clinically and radiographically confirmed ascites and right-sided pleural effusion, and a normal CA-125 (less suggestive of epithelial ovarian cancer). The pleural effusion being right-sided is typical for transdiaphragmatic passage of ascitic fluid seen in Meigs syndrome. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is a benign ovarian fibroma (or related stromal tumor) producing ascites and a reactive right pleural effusion (Meigs syndrome).

DIAGNOSIS: Meigs syndrome (ovarian fibroma with ascites and right-sided pleural effusion)
